messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Eduardo was sixty-seven years old, a widower for nearly a decade, and a prosecutor who had spent forty years in the same downtown courthouse. He was known for his quiet intensity, for never raising his voice in the courtroom, for the way he could sit through a cross-examination without shifting in his chair. But that composure had been hollow for the last two years—ever since the night that rewired everything he thought he knew about safety, about his own body, about the world.

The assault happened in the parking garage beneath his office building. He had stayed late to review a file, a routine thing, and walked to his car at a little past nine. The air was cool and damp, a specific temperature on his skin that he would later come to dread—not cold enough to shiver, but enough to make the hairs on his arms stand up. He had noticed a man leaning against a pillar near his car, but he had dismissed it. He was a prosecutor; he dealt with dangerous people every day in a controlled environment. This was different. The man grabbed him from behind, pressed something sharp against his ribs, and forced him into the back seat of his own vehicle. What happened in the next forty minutes Eduardo could describe with a clarity that felt like a curse. He remembered every sound, every smell, every word the man said. The memory did not fade or soften. It remained as vivid as the moment it happened, and it would force its way into his mind without warning—during a deposition, while he was eating dinner alone, in the middle of the night. And when it came, it did not feel like a memory. It felt like it was happening right now, again, and he could do nothing to stop it.

In the weeks afterward, Eduardo tried to return to his normal routine. He went back to the courthouse. He sat in his office. But something fundamental had shifted. He began to feel that the world was a dangerous place in a way he had never truly understood before. He had always known crime intellectually, had built a career on prosecuting it. Now he felt it in his bones. He started scanning every room he entered for exits—the courthouse chambers, the grocery store, even his own living room. He could not help noticing potential weapons everywhere: a letter opener on a desk, a pair of scissors in a drawer, a heavy lamp. He became acutely aware of his body, too. He felt dirty, contaminated in a way that no amount of showering could fix. He was certain that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, even though the physical injuries had healed. He could not articulate exactly what was wrong, only that something inside him was broken and would never be whole again.

His occupation became a minefield. As a prosecutor, Eduardo had to meet with victims, with witnesses, with defense attorneys in unfamiliar conference rooms. He began to avoid those meetings whenever possible, delegating them to junior colleagues. He would not go to any place he had not already assessed for danger. When he did have to enter a new building, he would arrive early, walk the perimeter, locate every exit, and still feel a knot of tension that did not ease until he left. The presence of children became unbearable. He had grandchildren he loved, but being around them now made his skin crawl. He could not explain why. The sound of their laughter, the way they ran and played—it felt wrong, unsafe, as if the world could reach into that innocence at any moment. He stopped visiting his daughter's house.

The consequences accumulated slowly. His colleagues noticed his withdrawal. They saw him flinch when someone came up behind him, saw him refuse to attend the annual office party in a rented banquet hall. He stopped taking cases that required fieldwork or site visits. His caseload shrank. He began to worry that his career was ending not with a retirement ceremony but with a quiet erosion of everything he had been. He did not tell anyone why. He could not find the words.

What finally brought Eduardo to seek help was not a single crisis but a cumulative exhaustion. He had spent two years living in a state of constant vigilance, and he was tired. He sat in the therapist's office with his hands folded in his lap, his eyes fixed on the door, and said that he wanted to stop feeling like a prisoner in his own life. He was afraid that he would never feel clean again, never feel safe again, never walk into a room without counting the exits. But he was also afraid of what it would mean to let go of that vigilance—as if the only thing keeping him alive was the scanning, the noticing, the never relaxing. He did not know what he would be without it.
